content: Describe the night side of Earth as seen from orbit, where city lights trace coastlines, rivers and roads.
Describe looking at a distant galaxy as looking into the past, and convey how its light carries a history older than the Earth.
Describe a neutron star, where a spoonful of matter would outweigh a mountain, and convey how such density changes the rules of ordinary matter.
Would finding simple microbial life on another planet change how people think about life on Earth?
Describe a comet's long journey from the frozen outer solar system to the glowing tail it grows near the Sun.
Why do astronauts aboard an orbiting space station float, even though gravity at that height is still strong?
Write a scene in which an amateur astronomer realizes that a faint smudge in the eyepiece was not there the night before.
Explain why there must be infinitely many prime numbers, using an argument a curious teenager could follow.
Describe the number zero as an invention that changed how people count, trade and calculate.
Is mathematics discovered or invented? Explore one consideration on each side without settling the question.
Explain why a random sample of a thousand people can say something useful about a country of millions.
Explain why a long password made of ordinary words can be harder to guess than a short one full of symbols.
Describe the journey of a single email from the moment it is sent to the moment it appears on a screen on another continent.
Should software that makes decisions about people always be able to explain its reasons? Explore one tension in this question.
Describe how the street names of an old market town can still reveal what was once made and sold there.
Why did the printing press change who could take part in arguments about ideas?
Describe the building of a great cathedral across several generations, when no single worker would live to see it finished.
Why can a single line of poetry stay with someone for years while a whole novel fades from memory?
Describe how a familiar song changes in feeling when it is played slowly in a minor key.
Describe how a borrowed word travels from one language into another and gradually changes once it settles in.
Describe the inside of a beehive in winter, when the colony survives by clustering together and shivering to make heat.
Explain how a vaccine trains the immune system without causing the disease it protects against.
Describe the migration of monarch butterflies, a round trip so long that it takes several generations to complete.
Why do the leaves of many trees change color in autumn?
Should extinct species be brought back if science makes it possible? Explore what such an effort might gain and what it might overlook.
Is it possible to owe gratitude to someone who helped you without meaning to?
Can a perfect copy of a famous painting ever be as valuable as the original?
Describe the puzzle of a wooden ship that is repaired plank by plank for a century until none of its original timber remains, and convey why the puzzle is hard to settle.
Explain the difference between something being legal and something being right, using an everyday example.
Why do people tend to remember the beginning and end of a list better than the middle?
Describe the moment of falling asleep, when thoughts loosen and drift into dream-like images.
Why do people sometimes prefer a familiar disappointment to an uncertain improvement? Explore the roles of fear, habit and identity.
Write a scene in which a song playing in a shop suddenly returns someone to a forgotten summer.
Describe a glacier as a slow river of ice that carries the record of past winters.
Explain why some stretches of coastline erode quickly while others nearby barely change.
Describe a volcanic island from its first eruption to the arrival of plants, birds and eventually people.
Why does a spinning top stay upright while it spins quickly but topple as it slows down?
Describe a rainbow as sunlight that has been bent and sorted inside countless falling drops.
Why might a city with many empty homes still have people who cannot find anywhere to live?
Write a scene in which a market trader packs up a stall for the last time after forty years.
Describe the rings of Saturn as a thin, restless disk of ice that looks solid only from far away.
Explain how a spacecraft can use a planet's gravity to gain speed without burning extra fuel.
Describe the surface of Mars at dawn, from the thin pink sky to the frost that vanishes as the ground warms.
If people built a permanent settlement on the Moon, who should decide how its land and resources are used? Explore one tension without proposing a final plan.
Describe a total solar eclipse as experienced by a crowd in an open field, from the first bite out of the Sun to the sudden dusk.
Why does the Moon always show the same face to Earth?
Write a scene in which two researchers at a remote observatory argue quietly about whether a strange reading is worth waking the director for.
Describe the idea of infinity through the image of a hotel with endless rooms that is completely full yet can always take one more guest.
Explain why dividing a number by zero has no sensible answer.
Why do mathematicians value an elegant proof even when a longer proof already shows the same result is true?
Explain what it means for two quantities to be correlated without one causing the other, using an everyday example.
Explain why a computer can sort a million names faster than a person could sort a hundred.
Describe the inside of a data center at night, where rows of machines hum and blink while most of the world sleeps.
Can a machine that composes music be called creative? Explore what we mean by creativity when we ask the question.
Describe an ancient road whose stones have been worn into grooves by centuries of cart wheels.
Explain how historians can estimate the population of an ancient city that left no census.
Why do people keep and pass down objects that have no practical use, such as a grandparent's broken watch? Explore what such objects carry.
Describe how a dancer can tell a whole story without a single spoken word.
Why do some words seem to sound like what they mean, such as buzz or whisper?
Describe the restoration of a faded mural, as conservators uncover colors that no living person has seen.
Describe a coral reef at night, when the daytime colors fade and hidden creatures emerge.
Explain how a tiny change in a single gene can make a large difference to how an organism looks or behaves.
Describe the life of a tree across five hundred years, measured in rings, storms and the creatures it has sheltered.
Why do some animals sleep through the winter while others stay active?
Should people try to protect every species from extinction, or accept that some loss is part of how nature changes? Explore one difficulty with each view.
Is a promise made under pressure still a promise?
Does a person whose good outcome came from luck deserve less praise than one who planned it?
Describe the experience of making a difficult choice as standing at a fork in a road where both paths disappear into fog.
Explain the difference between knowing that something is true and believing it for good reasons.
Why does time seem to pass more quickly as people grow older?
Describe what happens in the mind when a word is on the tip of the tongue but will not come.
Can people ever truly know what another person is feeling? Explore what empathy can and cannot reach.
Write a scene in which someone recognizes a stranger's laugh across a crowded train platform.
Describe a desert after a rare heavy rain, when dormant seeds and creatures burst into life.
Explain how ocean currents carry heat around the planet and why that matters for climate.
Describe the slow formation of a cave over thousands of years, from the first trickle of water to stalactites and echoing chambers.
Why does a straw look bent when it stands in a glass of water?
Describe sound as a traveling ripple of pressure by following a single clap across a quiet valley.
Why can a rule that treats everyone exactly the same still feel unfair to some people?
Write a scene in which neighbors gather in the street during a power cut and talk to each other properly for the first time.
Describe the light of a star that may no longer exist by the time it reaches someone looking up tonight.
Explain how scientists can tell what a distant star is made of without ever going there.
Describe the birth of a star inside a cold cloud of gas and dust, from slow collapse to the first ignition.
Should humanity send messages into space announcing its presence, or listen quietly first? Explore one argument on each side.
Describe a probe drifting through the outer solar system, photographing small icy worlds that have barely changed since the planets formed.
Why is the night sky dark even though there are countless stars?
Write a scene in which a family watches a rocket launch from a distant beach, each of them thinking about something different.
Explain why, in a room of just twenty-three people, the chance that two share a birthday is better than even.
Describe a spiral seashell as a shape that keeps growing without changing its form.
Can a mathematical model of a city's traffic ever be true, or only useful? Explore what models leave out and why that can be a strength.
Explain how rounding small amounts many times can add up to a large error.
Explain why a digital file can be copied perfectly while copies of a cassette tape slowly lose quality.
Describe the internet as a web of undersea cables, switching stations and blinking lights that most people never see.
Should old websites and digital records be preserved forever, even when the people who made them would prefer them forgotten?
Why did so many ancient cities grow up beside rivers?
Describe a nineteenth-century lighthouse keeper's daily routine, when the light depended entirely on human hands.
How should a museum decide whether to return an object to the community it was taken from? Explore the values that pull in different directions.
Describe how a photograph can freeze a moment that no one present noticed at the time.
Describe how a child picks up a new language by playing every day with children who speak it.
Can a translation of a poem become a new poem in its own right?
Describe an octopus changing color and texture as it moves across the sea floor.
Explain why antibiotics stop working well when bacteria are exposed to them too often.
Describe the hidden life in a handful of garden soil, from earthworms to microbes, and how it keeps plants alive.
Why do people get goosebumps when they are cold or deeply moved by music?
If science could greatly extend the human lifespan, should it? Explore what a much longer life might change for individuals and for societies.
Is it wrong to tell a comforting lie to someone who is dying?
Describe the idea that the present moment is all we ever directly experience, using the image of a single footprint on a beach.
Explain the difference between being free to act as you want and being free to choose what you want, using a simple example.
Can someone be responsible for a harm they could not have foreseen?
Why do people sometimes see faces in clouds, rocks or electrical outlets?
Describe reading a gripping book late at night, when the room disappears and the story takes over.
Does boredom serve a purpose? Explore what might be lost if people were never bored.
Write a scene in which an elderly musician whose memory is fading sits at a piano and finds that their hands still remember.
Describe the moment a thunderstorm breaks over dry fields after weeks of heat.
Explain how scientists learn about past climates from air bubbles trapped in ancient ice.
Describe a mangrove forest as a place where land and sea renegotiate their boundary twice a day.
Why does a heavy steel ship float while a small pebble sinks?
Describe magnetism as an invisible force by following iron filings as they arrange themselves around a magnet.
Explain why prices in a shop can rise even when nothing about the products has changed.
Write a scene in which a librarian helps a stranger find a book they only half remember.
Describe the aurora as seen from a frozen lake, where particles from the Sun meet the upper atmosphere.
Explain how astronomers know that the universe is expanding.
Describe Jupiter's Great Red Spot as a storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries.
Why do planets keep orbiting the Sun instead of falling straight into it?
Describe what a sunset might look like on a planet that orbits two suns.
Is exploring space worth its cost when there are urgent problems on Earth? Explore one tension honestly.
Write a scene in which a child at a planetarium show asks a question that silences the presenter for a moment.
Describe the idea of mathematical symmetry through the image of a snowflake, where every arm repeats the others.
Explain why multiplying a negative number by a negative number gives a positive number.
Why do some people find mathematics beautiful while others find it cold? Explore what beauty in mathematics might mean.
Explain what a weather forecast means when it gives a seventy percent chance of rain, and what that number does not tell you.
Describe a single pixel on a screen as a tiny window that changes color many times every second.
Explain why recognizing a cat in a photograph is hard for a computer even though a toddler does it easily.
Should people be able to delete everything a company has stored about them? Explore one tension in this question.
Describe a caravan on an ancient trade route crossing a desert, carrying goods, languages and ideas between distant cultures.
Why did early mapmakers sometimes draw islands that later sailors could never find?
How do festivals keep old traditions alive while changing them with each generation? Explore whether a tradition that keeps changing is still the same tradition.
Explain how rhyme and rhythm can make a sentence easier to remember.
Describe the silence just before an orchestra begins to play, and how it shapes what the audience hears next.
Is a story still the same story when it is retold with a different ending?
Describe a spider spinning its web at dawn, thread by thread, in a few patient minutes.
Explain how the human eye adjusts when someone walks from bright sunlight into a dark room.
Describe a salmon's return upstream to the river where it hatched, guided by the memory of a smell.
Why do some plants fold their leaves at night?
Do animals experience joy? Explore what kind of evidence could count and why the question is so hard to answer.
Is it better to admit a mistake that no one would ever discover?
Describe the idea of fairness through the image of two children dividing a cake.
Explain how a thought experiment can teach us something even though it describes a situation that could never happen.
Is a life well lived one that is happy, one that is meaningful, or something else? Explore one tension.
Why do people often yawn after seeing someone else yawn?
Describe the experience of déjà vu, when a new moment feels strangely like a memory.
Are habits a kind of freedom, because they free our attention, or a kind of cage? Explore both sides.
Write a scene in which someone finds an old note in their own handwriting that they do not remember writing.
Describe the first snowfall of winter settling on a busy city and briefly quieting it.
Explain why earthquakes happen much more often in some parts of the world than in others.
Describe a rainforest canopy as a world above the world, from the tops of the tallest trees down to the shaded forest floor.
Why does a microwave oven heat soup quickly while the bowl often stays cooler?
Describe the moment a kettle begins to sing, as bubbles of steam form and collapse at the bottom of the water.
Why do people trust a recommendation from a friend more than an advertisement?
Write a scene in which a newly arrived family tries to buy groceries in a country whose language they do not yet speak.
